claim: Hemoglobin (Hb) represents a model protein to study molecular adaptation in vertebrates.
source: Hemoglobin (Hb) represents a model protein to study molecular adaptation in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing Hb as a model system for studying adaptation.

claim: Both affinity and cooperativity of oxygen binding to Hb affect tissue oxygen delivery.
source: Although both affinity and cooperativity of oxygen binding to Hb affect tissue oxygen delivery, only the former was thought to determine molecular adaptations of Hb.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hb function.

claim: Only affinity was thought to determine molecular adaptations of Hb.
source: Although both affinity and cooperativity of oxygen binding to Hb affect tissue oxygen delivery, only the former was thought to determine molecular adaptations of Hb.
evidence: This reflects the historical view in the field prior to this study.

claim: Mammalian Hb cooperativity values all reside on a ridge of maximum cooperativity along the biophysical Hill landscape.
source: We found that mammalian Hb cooperativity values all reside on a ridge of maximum cooperativity along this landscape that allows for both gross- and fine-tuning of tissue oxygen unloading to meet the distinct metabolic requirements of mammalian tissues for oxygen.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on mapping experimental data onto the theoretical landscape.

claim: The ridge of maximum cooperativity allows for both gross- and fine-tuning of tissue oxygen unloading.
source: We found that mammalian Hb cooperativity values all reside on a ridge of maximum cooperativity along this landscape that allows for both gross- and fine-tuning of tissue oxygen unloading to meet the distinct metabolic requirements of mammalian tissues for oxygen.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical analysis and experimental data mapping.

claim: Mutation and selection are separated by several levels of biological organization.
source: One stems from the fact that mutation and selection are separated by several levels of biological organization such that it is difficult to elucidate the complex relationships between protein sequence and organismal/population fitness.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in evolutionary biology.

claim: It is difficult to elucidate the complex relationships between protein sequence and organismal/population fitness.
source: One stems from the fact that mutation and selection are separated by several levels of biological organization such that it is difficult to elucidate the complex relationships between protein sequence and organismal/population fitness.
evidence: This is stated as a general challenge in the field.

claim: We currently understand the mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior for only a very limited number of proteins.
source: Given these challenges, we currently understand the mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior for only a very limited number of proteins (e.g. Mello and Tu, 2005; Keymer et al., 2006; Swem et al., 2008; Storz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific examples in the literature.

claim: Hb is a tetrameric allosteric protein responsible for tissue oxygen delivery.
source: Hb is a tetrameric allosteric protein responsible for tissue oxygen delivery in a manner controlled by the midpoint and slope of its oxygen saturation curve.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hb structure and function.

claim: Tissue oxygen delivery by Hb is controlled by the midpoint and slope of its oxygen saturation curve.
source: Hb is a tetrameric allosteric protein responsible for tissue oxygen delivery in a manner controlled by the midpoint and slope of its oxygen saturation curve.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hb function.

claim: The macroscopic parameters p50 and nH reflect the effective affinity and cooperativity of oxygen binding by Hb, respectively.
source: These macroscopic parameters reflect the effective affinity (p50) and cooperativity (nH) of oxygen binding by Hb, respectively and are traditionally evaluated using the Hill equation, derived assuming an all-or-none mode of binding (Hill, 1910).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hill's original work and is established knowledge.

claim: Hb oxygen affinity (p50) is an adaptive trait.
source: Over the years, many studies have indicated that Hb oxygen affinity (p50) is an adaptive trait, that is its value has been tuned during evolution so as to tailor tissue oxygen delivery to the particular metabolic requirements of vertebrates due to variations in body size, lifestyle and/or environmental conditions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple studies cited in the text.

claim: Vertebrates native to mountain habitats usually possess Hb that exhibits higher affinity for oxygen than does the Hb of lowland dwellers.
source: For example, vertebrates native to mountain habitats where low ambient oxygen pressures prevail usually possess Hb that exhibits higher affinity for oxygen than does the Hb of lowland dwellers (Lenfant, 1973; Bunn, 1980; Weber, 2007; Storz and Moriyama, 2008; Storz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hb in small-sized animals that display high metabolic rates presents lower affinity for oxygen than does the same protein in large-sized animals.
source: Likewise, Hb in small-sized animals that display high metabolic rates presents lower affinity for oxygen than does the same protein in large-sized animals, again reflecting the adaptive adjustment of tissue oxygen unloading by Hb (Schmidt-Neilsen and Larimer, 1958; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt-Nielsen's work.

claim: Early respiratory system physiologists assigned great significance to the p50 parameter, terming it 'oxygen unloading tension'.
source: Accordingly, early respiratory system physiologists assigned great significance to the p50 parameter, terming it 'oxygen unloading tension', and proposed that Hb function could be explained in terms of adaptive evolution of this value (Schmidt-Neilsen and Larimer, 1958; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work.

claim: Early studies ignored the adaptive potential of cooperativity (nH) with respect to Hb function.
source: At the same time, such studies ignored the adaptive potential of cooperativity (nH) with respect to Hb function.
evidence: This is stated as a historical gap in the field.

claim: nH also affects Hb tissue oxygen delivery.
source: This is surprising, given that nH also affects Hb tissue oxygen delivery.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hb function.

claim: Mechanisms underlying changes in p50 are all also expected to affect nH.
source: Moreover, mechanisms underlying changes in p50, such as changes in oxygen affinity of the oxy- or deoxy-states of Hb, changes in the ratio between these states or changes in their sensitivity to allosteric effectors, are all also expected to affect nH.
evidence: This is inferred from the biophysical properties of the MWC model.

claim: Mammalian Hbs exhibit variations in the Hill cooperativity value.
source: Indeed, the finding by Milo et al. (2007) that mammalian Hbs exhibit variations in the Hill cooperativity value hints at the adaptive potential of the nH trait.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Milo et al. (2007).

claim: There is an inherent tradeoff between arterial O2 loading and peripheral O2 unloading.
source: Given the inherent tradeoff between arterial O2 loading and peripheral O2 unloading, it is not clear whether improved tissue oxygen delivery is achieved by increased oxygen affinity to improve Hb loading or by decreased affinity to favor unloading (Storz, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known principle with citation support.

claim: Very high or very low oxygen affinity would result in a low fraction of tissue oxygen delivery unless cooperativity (nH) between Hb subunits is introduced.
source: Either very high or very low oxygen affinity would result in a low fraction of tissue oxygen delivery unless cooperativity (nH) between Hb subunits is introduced as a means to switch between low- and high-affinity Hb states.
evidence: This is inferred from basic principles of Hb function.

claim: The values of both p50 and nH of Hb should reflect physiological optimization of the tradeoff between O2 loading in the lungs and O2 unloading in tissues.
source: It would thus seem that the values of both p50 and nH of Hb should reflect physiological optimization of the tradeoff between O2 loading in the lungs and O2 unloading in tissues, so as to optimize tissue oxygen delivery.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, based on logical inference.

claim: The evolutionary dataset comprises a set of oxygen binding curves of homologous Hb proteins from different mammalian species, all measured under similar physiological conditions.
source: The former comprises a set of oxygen binding curves of homologous Hb proteins from different mammalian species, all measured under similar physiological conditions (Milo et al., 2007; Rapp and Yifrach, 2017).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study with citation support.

claim: The physiological dataset comprises a set of binding curves of human Hb measured under a variety of different physiological conditions.
source: The latter comprises a set of binding curves of human Hb measured under a variety of different physiological conditions, that is, in the presence of different concentrations of H+, CO2 and organophosphate, all inhibitory allosteric ligands of Hb (Rapp and Yifrach, 2017).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study with citation support.

claim: H+, CO2 and organophosphate are all inhibitory allosteric ligands of Hb.
source: The latter comprises a set of binding curves of human Hb measured under a variety of different physiological conditions, that is, in the presence of different concentrations of H+, CO2 and organophosphate, all inhibitory allosteric ligands of Hb (Rapp and Yifrach, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hb regulation.

claim: Reliable estimates for p50 and nH Hill parameters and for the elementary relative affinity (c) and conformational changes (L) parameters of the MWC model are available for all dataset curves.
source: For all data sets curves, reliable estimates for p50 and nH Hill parameters and for the elementary relative affinity (c) and conformational changes (L) parameters of the MWC concerted allosteric model (Monod et al., 1965; Rubin and Changeux, 1966) are available.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work where these parameters were derived.

claim: The Hb evolutionary dataset comprises 14 different mammalian Hb oxygen saturation curves obtained under similar physiological conditions.
source: Specifically, the Hb evolutionary dataset comprises 14 different mammalian Hb oxygen saturation curves obtained under similar physiological conditions (Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the specific dataset used in the study.

claim: The Hb physiological dataset comprises 26 different human Hb saturation curves collected under a variety of different physiological conditions.
source: The Hb physiological dataset comprises 26 different human Hb saturation curves collected under a variety of different physiological conditions, including those involving changes in H+ (Di Cera et al., 1988; Imai, 1983), CO2 (Doyle et al., 1987) and 2,3-BPG (bis-phosphoglycerate) (Benesch et al., 1971) concentrations.
evidence: This describes the specific dataset used with citation support.

claim: In the MWC model, tetrameric Hb is assumed to be in equilibrium between the un-liganded low-affinity T (tense or deoxy) and the high-affinity R (relaxed or oxy) states.
source: According to the MWC model, tetrameric Hb is assumed to be in equilibrium between the un-liganded low-affinity T (tense or deoxy) and the high-affinity R (relaxed or oxy) states, as described by the L allosteric constant (L=[T]/[R]).
evidence: This is a description of the MWC model as applied to Hb.

claim: In the classical MWC model, cooperativity in substrate binding (homotropic interactions) is determined by both L and c.
source: In the classical MWC model, cooperativity in substrate binding (homotropic interactions) is determined by both L and c (Monod et al., 1965).
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the MWC model with citation support.

claim: Heterotropic interactions, describing the effects of allosteric ligands on substrate binding, only affect the L parameter.
source: Heterotropic interactions, on the other hand, describing the effects of allosteric ligands on substrate binding, only affect the L parameter.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the MWC model.

claim: The calculated Hill values of all mammalian Hbs reside close to the maximum points of the bell-shaped contours of the three-dimensional Hill landscape.
source: When mapped onto the theoretical Hill landscape, the calculated Hill values of all mammalian Hbs reside close to the maximum points of the bell-shaped contours of the three-dimensional Hill landscape (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on mapping experimental data onto the theoretical landscape.

claim: The logarithms of the values for L and c of the different Hbs are linearly correlated with a slope value of −2.7 (±0.3).
source: Furthermore, the logarithms of the values for L and c of the different Hbs are linearly correlated (Figure 2b) with a slope value of −2.7 (±0.3), close to a value of −2 that would be expected for proteins that evolved to present maximum cooperativity in ligand binding (L = c -n/2).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: A slope value of −2 would be expected for proteins that evolved to present maximum cooperativity in ligand binding.
source: Furthermore, the logarithms of the values for L and c of the different Hbs are linearly correlated (Figure 2b) with a slope value of −2.7 (±0.3), close to a value of −2 that would be expected for proteins that evolved to present maximum cooperativity in ligand binding (L = c -n/2).
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical MWC model criterion for maximum cooperativity.

claim: The logL-logc correlation crosses very close to the (0,0) axis origin point.
source: The observation that the logL-logc correlation crosses very close to the (0,0) axis origin point further supports this assertion.
evidence: This is observed from the data analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: L and c are independent parameters of the MWC model.
source: Given that L and c are independent parameters of the MWC model, the logarithms of their values for a given protein set are not expected to be linearly-dependent.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the MWC model.

claim: The observed linearity between mammalian logL and logc values points to co-evolution of the two MWC parameters.
source: We thus suggest that the observed linearity between mammalian logL and logc values does not imply causation or is an artifact but rather points to co-evolution of the two MWC parameters so as to shape Hb cooperativity close to the maximum value.
evidence: This is inferred from the data pattern and theoretical considerations.

claim: A buffering of cooperativity regime is observed around a maximum cooperativity Hill point.
source: As highlighted above, a buffering of cooperativity regime is observed around a maximum cooperativity Hill point.
evidence: This is a property of the MWC model at maximum cooperativity.

claim: Minor changes in nH are to be expected upon changes in L brought about by the binding of allosteric inhibitors or activators around the maximum cooperativity point.
source: As such, minor changes in nH are to be expected upon changes in L brought about by the binding of allosteric inhibitors or activators.
evidence: This is a consequence of the buffering of cooperativity regime.

claim: logL-nH data points of the physiological dataset cluster around the maximum point of the bell-shaped curve.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3a, logL-nH data points of the physiological dataset (black symbols) cluster around the maximum point of the bell-shaped curve.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: This pattern is in sharp contrast to the scattered pattern of the pairs of logL-nH values for Hb mutants reported in the literature.
source: This pattern is in sharp contrast to the scattered pattern of the pairs of logL-nH values for Hb mutants reported in the literature (gray circles) (Baldwin, 1976) and assumed by Baldwin (1976) (and later by Fersht, 1985) to have the same c value.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the physiological dataset to literature data on mutants.

claim: Significant deviations from the maximum cooperativity value of wild-type human Hb were observed for naturally occurring Hb mutants, such as the Kansas and Chesapeake variants.
source: Significant deviations from the maximum cooperativity value of wild-type human Hb were also observed for naturally occurring Hb mutants, such as the Kansas and Chesapeake variants (Edelstein, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Edelstein's work.

claim: The clustering of all logL-nH experimental data points of the H+, CO2 and 2,3-BPG datasets around the maximum point reveals that the Hill value for human Hb is relatively insensitive to changes in physiological conditions.
source: The clustering of all logL-nH experimental data points of the H+, CO2 and 2,3-BPG datasets around the maximum point reveals that the Hill value for human Hb is relatively insensitive to changes in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the data pattern shown in Figure 3.

claim: nH-insensitive behavior was noted for the pH-related Bohr effect of Hb.
source: Such nH-insensitive behavior was noted for the pH-related Bohr effect of Hb (Wyman, 1964; Di Cera et al., 1988) and later extended to other allosteric effectors of Hb (Milo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The results provide a mechanistic explanation, based on the MWC model parameters, for the 'buffering of cooperativity' property of Hb.
source: Our results showing the invariance of nH with respect to logL thus provide a mechanistic explanation, based on the MWC model parameters, for the 'buffering of cooperativity' property of Hb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical and experimental results.

claim: Human Hb had evolved to present maximum cooperativity in oxygen binding.
source: Such behavior should only appear if human Hb had evolved to present maximum cooperativity in oxygen binding (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is inferred from the buffering of cooperativity behavior observed.

claim: Site-directed point mutants of Hb are not subjected to the selection pressure that leads to maximum cooperativity.
source: As site-directed point mutants of Hb are not subjected to the selection pressure that leads to maximum cooperativity, the values of logL-nH pairs for such mutants fall off the extremum point of the logL-nH cross-section (Baldwin, 1976).
evidence: This is inferred from evolutionary principles and supported by citation.

claim: The higher the value of the maximum Hill point of the appropriate binding curve, the more it is displaced to the right along the scaled concentration axis.
source: Under such conditions, the affinity and maximum Hill point are correlated (Figure 4a). The higher the value of the maximum Hill point of the appropriate binding curve, the more it is displaced to the right along the scaled concentration axis.
evidence: This is observed from the simulated curves in Figure 4a.

claim: There is monotonic correlation between the maximum Hill value and logα1/2.
source: This is reflected in Figure 4b, showing monotonic correlation between the maximum Hill value and logα1/2 (α1/2=[S]1/2/KR).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b based on theoretical calculations.

claim: Under the maximum cooperativity parameter condition, a tradeoff exists between the cooperativity and affinity properties of a MWC-type protein.
source: It thus seems that under the maximum cooperativity parameter condition, a tradeoff exist between the cooperativity and affinity properties of a MWC-type protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The value for the Δ$Y¯_{100 → 40%}$/Δlogα parameter increases monotonically in a power law manner with increases in the value of the maximum Hill point.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4c (filled black symbols), the value for this parameter increases monotonically in a power law manner with increases in the value of the maximum Hill point.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c based on theoretical calculations.

claim: Higher maximum Hill points ensure higher sensitivity for substrate unbinding by the MWC protein.
source: Higher maximum Hill points thus ensure higher sensitivity for substrate unbinding by the MWC protein.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Higher maximum Hill values give rise to broader L ranges, where 'buffering of cooperativity' is observed.
source: Plotting the dependence of ΔlogL on the maximum cooperativity Hill value (Figure 4f) reveals that higher maximum Hill values give rise to broader L ranges, where 'buffering of cooperativity' is observed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4f based on theoretical calculations.

claim: Within the buffering of cooperativity range, changes of up to 6% are observed in the value of protein unbinding sensitivity in response to changes in physiological conditions.
source: As can be seen, within this range, changes of up to 6% are observed in the value of protein unbinding sensitivity in response to changes in physiological conditions brought about by changes in L alone yet reflected in changes in p50 alone.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Different mammalian Hbs exhibit different maximum nH values.
source: The fact that different mammalian Hbs exhibit different maximum nH values (Figure 2a), combined with the observation made above whereby systematically higher maximum Hill value gives rise to higher sensitivities to substrate unloading by MWC proteins (Figure 4c), led us to hypothesize that the maximum cooperativity point of Hb has been tuned during evolution to satisfy the particular physiological requirements of different tissues for oxygen supply.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The maximum cooperativity point of Hb has been tuned during evolution to satisfy the particular physiological requirements of different tissues for oxygen supply.
source: The fact that different mammalian Hbs exhibit different maximum nH values (Figure 2a), combined with the observation made above whereby systematically higher maximum Hill value gives rise to higher sensitivities to substrate unloading by MWC proteins (Figure 4c), led us to hypothesize that the maximum cooperativity point of Hb has been tuned during evolution to satisfy the particular physiological requirements of different tissues for oxygen supply.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on combining observations from Figures 2a and 4c.

claim: The greater an animal's metabolic rate, the higher was the observed maximum Hill cooperativity value of oxygen binding by Hb.
source: Specifically, the greater an animal's metabolic rate, the higher was the observed maximum Hill cooperativity value of oxygen binding by Hb.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: An inverse linear correlation was found between the metabolic rate and Hb affinity.
source: Furthermore, as previously shown (Schmidt-Neilsen and Larimer, 1958; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1970), an inverse linear correlation was found between the metabolic rate and Hb affinity.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 5c and supported by citations.

claim: These empirical observations directly relate the maximum cooperativity and affinity properties of Hb to an organismal-level trait that is related to fitness.
source: These empirical observations directly relate the maximum cooperativity and affinity properties of Hb to an organismal-level trait that is related to fitness (Dykhuizen et al., 1987; Kacser and Burns, 1981; Bershtein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is concluded from the correlations shown in Figure 5c with citation support.

claim: Mammalian Hb nH and p50 values reflect evolutionary and physiological adaptations that serve to optimize the tradeoff between O2 loading in pulmonary capillaries and O2 unloading in tissue capillaries.
source: Taken together, these points support the assertion that mammalian Hb nH and p50 values reflect evolutionary and physiological adaptations that serve to optimize the tradeoff between O2 loading in pulmonary capillaries and O2 unloading in tissue capillaries, so as to optimize tissue oxygen delivery.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the evidence presented.

claim: Evolutionary (i.e., across species) variations allow for gross changes in Hb oxygen unloading sensitivity.
source: Based on experimental (Figures 2 and 3) and theoretical (Figure 4) results, we suggest that evolutionary (i.e., across species) variations allow for gross changes in Hb oxygen unloading sensitivity.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental and theoretical results.

claim: Such gross changes are controlled by the maximum cooperativity and affinity values of Hb, in turn determined by changes in both L and c.
source: Such changes are controlled by the maximum cooperativity and affinity values of Hb, in turn determined by changes in both L and c (Figure 4c, filled symbols).
evidence: This is concluded from the theoretical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Fine-tuning changes in Hb oxygen unloading sensitivity may be brought about by physiological variations within the buffering of cooperativity regime, reflected in changes in L and p50 alone.
source: Fine-tuning changes in Hb oxygen unloading sensitivity may further be brought about by physiological variations within the buffering of cooperativity regime, this time, however, reflected in changes in L and p50 alone (Figure 4c, open symbols).
evidence: This is concluded from the theoretical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The linear dependence between the metabolic rate of an animal and the maximum Hill value for Hb indicates that nH carries adaptive value with respect to mammalian Hb tissue oxygen unloading.
source: The linear dependence between the metabolic rate of an animal and the maximum Hill value for Hb (Figure 5c), combined with the results presented in Figure 4c, indicates that nH, like p50, carries adaptive value with respect to mammalian Hb tissue oxygen unloading.
evidence: This is concluded from combining the results in Figures 5c and 4c.

claim: Small body-sized animals presenting high metabolic rates require high oxygen supplies that can be more efficiently delivered by Hb presenting higher maximum Hill values.
source: As such, small body-sized animals presenting high metabolic rates require high oxygen supplies that can be more efficiently delivered by Hb presenting higher maximum Hill values.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between metabolic rate and maximum Hill value.

claim: Both the affinity and cooperativity traits of Hb represent low dimensional components of the fitness landscape.
source: Considering that an animal's metabolic rate is a trait related to organism fitness, we suggest that both the affinity and cooperativity traits of Hb represent low dimensional components of the fitness landscape, independent of other components.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between Hb properties and metabolic rate.

claim: The biophysical nH landscape of Hb can be regarded as a biophysical fitness landscape.
source: In this respect, the biophysical nH landscape of Hb can be regarded as a biophysical fitness landscape that serves to bridge the genotype-phenotype gap in assessing the relation between sequence variations in Hb (that affect its affinity and cooperativity properties) and their ensuing fitness effects (Bershtein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion with citation support.

claim: Evolutionary tuning of mammalian Hb maximum cooperativity and affinity points regulates tissue oxygen delivery by Hb and serves as one mean to meet the distinct needs of different animal tissues for oxygen.
source: Evolutionary tuning of mammalian Hb maximum cooperativity and affinity points, achieved by co-varying the relative affinity and conformational ratio of its quaternary states, thus regulates tissue oxygen delivery by Hb and serves as one mean to meet the distinct needs of different animal tissues for oxygen (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Other mechanisms related to cardiac output and to convective and diffusive steps in the oxygen transport pathway also contribute to modulation of tissue oxygen transport.
source: Clearly, other mechanisms related to cardiac output and to convective and diffusive steps in the oxygen transport pathway are as well contribute to modulation of tissue oxygen transport (reviewed in Schmidt-Nielsen, 1975).
evidence: This is acknowledged with citation support.

claim: The capillary density of a mammal is inversely correlated to body size.
source: For example, it has been shown that the capillary density of a mammal is also inversely correlated to body size (Schmidt-Nielsen, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt-Nielsen's work.

claim: The buffering of cooperativity regime in Hb reflects the case where the fractional saturation curves of the protein seem parallel in shape and are only displaced along the substrate concentration axis in response to changes in effector ligand concentrations.
source: The buffering of cooperativity regime in Hb reflects the case where the fractional saturation curves of the protein seem parallel in shape and are only displaced along the substrate concentration axis in response to changes in effector ligand concentrations (see Figure 4e).
evidence: This is observed from the simulated curves in Figure 4e.

claim: This behavior qualifies a MWC protein as a logarithmic sensor, reflecting the capacity of the protein to respond identically over a broad range of changes in chemical potential.
source: As revealed by Olsman and Goentoro (2016), it is exactly this behavior the qualifies a MWC protein as a logarithmic sensor, reflecting the capacity of the protein to respond identically over a broad range of changes in chemical potential.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olsman and Goentoro (2016).

claim: Many MWC allosteric proteins exhibit a buffering of cooperativity or logarithmic sensing regime in response to changes in the concentration of the modulatory allosteric signal.
source: Upon surveying the literature, Olsman and Goentoro (2016) found that many MWC allosteric proteins, including phosphofructokinase, Hb, cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels, Tar receptors, G-protein coupled receptors and EGF receptors exhibit a buffering of cooperativity or logarithmic sensing regime in response to changes in the concentration (or magnitude) of the modulatory allosteric signal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olsman and Goentoro (2016).

claim: The dynamic range for buffering of cooperativity behavior can vary from 10-fold (Hb) to 10,000-fold (GPCR).
source: The dynamic range for this behavior can vary from 10-fold (Hb) to 10,000-fold (GPCR).
evidence: This is stated based on literature survey results.

claim: All these MWC proteins evolved to present maximum cooperativity values in ligand binding and operate under the L = c -n/2 parameter regime.
source: These findings suggest that all these MWC proteins evolved to present maximum cooperativity values in ligand binding and operate under the L = c -n/2 parameter regime that gives rise to the buffering of cooperativity phenomenon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of buffering of cooperativity in multiple proteins.

claim: Other than Hb, the significance of maximum cooperativity to organismal fitness is known only in the case of a single protein.
source: However, other than Hb, the significance of this finding to organismal fitness is known only in the case of a single protein (Keymer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The roadmap that underlies the 'biophysical Hill landscape'-mapping strategy is general and can be applied to reveal the relation between evolutionary and physiological variations in shaping any molecular property of a protein.
source: Finally, the roadmap that underlies the 'biophysical Hill landscape'-mapping strategy is general and can be applied to reveal the relation between evolutionary (i.e. sequence) and physiological (e.g. changes in metabolite concentrations) variations in shaping any molecular property of a protein.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the applicability of the approach.

claim: The functional data analyzed considered the evolutionary and physiology Hb datasets respectively compiled in Milo et al. (2007) and Rapp and Yifrach (2017).
source: The functional data analyzed here considered the evolutionary and physiology Hb datasets respectively complied in Milo et al. (2007) and Rapp and Yifrach (2017).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The physiological dataset comprised four independent human Hb sub-datasets, obtained from three different labs.
source: The physiological dataset comprised four independent human Hb sub-datasets, obtained from three different labs, with two reporting pH modulation, one considering CO2 modulation and the last addressing 2,3-BPG modulation, as discussed in the meta analyses by Rapp and Yifrach (2017).
evidence: This describes the composition of the physiological dataset.
